 What are the relevant questions?

 Different analysis techniques answer (or fail to answer) different, but
 often related, questions—it is critical to understanding these
 different questions.
 Answers to these different questions often lead to different uses.
 Starting with the right questions simplifies both the development of
 appropriate analyses and motivating the proper use of the results.
 However, the “right questions” often vary by stakeholder group.
 Identifying the questions you will answer sets the stage for
 subsequent conversations that will take place.
 Yen (2007), from a state survey of parents, teachers and
 administrators, compiled a list of frequently voiced
 questions/concerns for each group.

 Why Growth for School Accountability?

 A fundamental premise associated with using student growth for
 school accountability is that “good” schools bring about student
 growth in excess of that found at “bad” schools.
 The inherent believability of this premise is at the heart of current
 enthusiasm to incorporate growth models into state accountability
 systems.
 Students attending such schools—commonly referred to as highly
 effective/ineffective schools—tend to demonstrate extraordinary
 growth that is causally attributed to the school or teachers instructing
 the students.

 Value-added Models/Inferences
 The primary thrust of growth analyses has been to determine, using
 sophisticated statistical techniques, the amount of student
 progress/growth that can be justifiably attributed to the school or
 teacher.
 Such analyses, often called value-added analyses, attempt to
 estimate the teacher/school contribution to student achievement.
 Value-added models provide effectiveness quantities that purport to
 quantify the impact on achievement that this school or teacher would
 have, on average, upon similar students assigned to them.
 The foremost example being the value-added models developed by
 Dr. William Sanders and used in many districts and states
 nationwide to infer teacher or school effectiveness.
 These models and their effectiveness claims are controversial for a
 number of reasons [Braun, 2005, Rubin et al., 2004].
 Value-added models are better described as effectiveness than as
 growth models.

 Actual versus Aspirational Student Growth

 It seems simple enough: Establish what constitutes a year’s growth
 in a year’s time for each student.
 This simplicity belies a subtle complexity.
 To adequately address the notion of a year’s growth, actual growth
 must be distinguished from aspirational growth.
 Describe What is a current year’s growth?
 Prescribe What should a current year’s growth be?
 Answering the second question establishes a threshold
 distinguishing adequate from inadequate growth.
 To make such a distinction requires an answer to the first question
 which defines a norm: What is the range of growth currently
 observed?
 Aspirational growth should be possible—This is Linn’s existence
 proof applied at the individual level [Linn, 2003].

 Describing Actual Student Growth

 Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
 task.
 Numerous States believe that placing their tests on a vertical scale
 will simplify the task of measuring student growth.
 Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
 Consider, for example, height.
 A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
 4 inches is a well understood quantity.
 However, the 4 inch increase becomes fully understandable only when
 placed in context of growth of other children between ages 3 and 4.
 In the following discussion student growth percentiles are introduced
 to provide a normative context for interpreting student growth.

 Student Growth Percentiles
 As the figures indicate, there is a distribution of 2006 scale scores
 associated with each 2005 scale score.
 The average (or median) of the conditional density could be used as
 a point estimate of the expected 2006 scale score given the student’s
 2005 performance.
 Similarly, the middle 50% of each density gives a range of scores
 where one would expect such a student’s score to reside 50% of the
 time.
 Using quantile regression techniques, conditional densities using
 more than a single prior score can be estimated.
 Given a student’s prior scale scores and the associated conditional
 density, their current scale score corresponds to a percentile of that
 conditional distribution.
 This percentile is the student’s growth percentile.
 For example, a student growth percentile of 60 indicates the student’s
 latest scale score exceeded 60 percent of his/her counterparts with
 equal prior scores.

 Student Growth Percentiles
 Student growth percentiles norm each student’s growth relative to
 their academic peers.
 The growth percentiles are estimated using quantile regression
 techniques (Betebenner & Shang, 2007; Koenker, 2005).
 The percentile scale on which the growth percentiles lie allows for
 easy comparison of all students.
 For example, consider a low achieving student demonstrating 90th
 percentile growth and a high achieving student demonstrating 10th
 percentile growth.
 The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 90 percent of similar
 students.
 The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 10 percent of
 similar students.
 In this sense, the low achiever’s growth is more exemplary than the high
 achiever’s.
 However, judgment of whether the student’s growth was adequate
 requires external criteria.
